name: The paradoxical weakening of clerical power by Protestant theology
plain_explanation: Even though Luther and Calvin were just as dogmatic as Catholic theologians, their doctrines (abolishing purgatory, rejecting indulgences, teaching predestination) removed the mechanisms by which priests could claim to influence an individual's salvation. This meant Protestant Churches, even in Protestant countries, never became as powerful as the Catholic Church was in Catholic countries.
precise_definition: Russell's claim: 'These innovations, while they helped in the struggle with the Pope, prevented the Protestant Churches from becoming as powerful in Protestant countries as the Catholic Church was in Catholic countries. Protestant divines were... just as bigoted as Catholic theologians, but they had less power, and were therefore less able to do harm.'
why_it_mattered: It explains why, despite equally dogmatic clergy on both sides, Protestant countries developed more intellectual liberty over time -- not because Protestant theologians were more tolerant in spirit, but because their doctrines structurally reduced institutional clerical power.
historical_origin: A direct consequence of the theological choices of the early Reformation.
examples: Abolition of purgatory (removing the rationale for paid masses for the dead)
Rejection of Indulgences (removing a major source of papal revenue)
influence_on_later_thinkers: Sets up the following chapter's account of why the seventeenth-century scientific revolution found more room to flourish, and eventually more tolerance, in Protestant countries such as Holland and England.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central: theology here is shown determining institutional political power, not just personal belief.
